title: Missions grow up in phases
text: NASA projects move through a life cycle that starts with Pre-Phase A concept studies and continues through definition, design and development, and finally operations in Phase E.
sourceLocations: Design and Develop Science Missions webinar slides (NTRS 20250002492), project life cycle section

title: How mature is your idea?
text: JPL created Concept Maturity Levels (CMLs) to classify how mature a space mission concept is before it enters formal project formulation.
sourceLocations: Wessen et al. 2013, abstract (NTRS 20150007816)

title: Maturity in many dimensions
text: The CML matrix tracks a concept's maturity across several dimensions at once, including science objectives, mission design, technical risk, project organization and cost.
sourceLocations: Wessen et al. 2013, abstract (NTRS 20150007816)

title: CMLs 1 to 4
text: CMLs 1 through 4 describe the earliest, Pre-Phase A stage of a mission idea, before formal project formulation begins.
sourceLocations: Wessen et al. 2013, abstract (NTRS 20150007816)

title: Designing together
text: NASA Goddard's Mission Design Lab is a collaborative engineering environment where a team of specialists develops spaceflight mission and architecture concepts.
sourceLocations: Mission Design Lab page, introduction

title: A design in six days
text: A Mission Design Lab point design study lasts about six days and produces products such as CAD models, a master equipment list and a cost estimate.
sourceLocations: Mission Design Lab page, 'Study types and timeframes' (Point Design Study)

title: Studies matched to maturity
text: Goddard's design studies can be tailored to help a concept mature anywhere from CML 1 to CML 4, from a one-hour brainstorm to a full point design.
sourceLocations: Mission Design Lab page, 'Range of study options' and 'Study types and timeframes'

title: Every subsystem has a budget
text: During a Mission Design Lab study, each subsystem team produces its own design, trade studies, and estimates of mass, power and data rate, plus a risk assessment.
sourceLocations: Mission Design Lab page, study process description

title: A team of specialists
text: Mission Design Lab engineers cover disciplines such as power systems, propulsion, thermal, communications, flight dynamics and attitude control.
sourceLocations: Mission Design Lab page, 'MDL Disciplines'

title: Orbits all the way to the Moon
text: The Mission Design Lab designs orbits for many destinations, including low Earth orbit, geosynchronous orbit, libration points, lunar missions and deep space.
sourceLocations: Mission Design Lab page, 'MDL Capabilities'

title: Free mission-design software
text: GMAT, the General Mission Analysis Tool, is NASA's open-source software for space mission design, optimization and navigation.
sourceLocations: NASA Software Catalog, GSC-19640-1 (GMAT R2026) description

title: From Earth orbit to the Moon and beyond
text: GMAT supports missions in flight regimes ranging from low Earth orbit to lunar, libration point and deep-space missions.
sourceLocations: NASA Software Catalog, GSC-19640-1 description; GMAT Wiki Home

title: Click or code
text: Mission designers can drive GMAT through a graphical interface, its own scripting language, or from Python or Java.
sourceLocations: NASA Software Catalog, GSC-19640-1 description

title: Building a mission in software
text: In GMAT you build a mission from resources such as spacecraft, propagators, estimators and optimizers to model, optimize and estimate trajectories.
sourceLocations: GMAT Wiki Home (gmat.atlassian.net)

title: Planning engine burns
text: Flight dynamics teams use GMAT for real operations: the GMAT Wiki notes that teams for missions such as the Roman Space Telescope plan to use it as their primary maneuver-planning tool.
sourceLocations: GMAT Wiki Home (gmat.atlassian.net), mission usage notes

title: Science comes first
text: NASA's telescope learning game teaches that science requirements drive a telescope mission's design and engineering: you pick a science question first, then the wavelengths, instruments and optics to answer it.
sourceLocations: NASA Science 'Build It Yourself' game page, description

title: Not every combination works
text: In 'Build It Yourself', some instrument and optics options are unavailable because they would not be scientifically or technologically viable for the chosen science goal.
sourceLocations: NASA Science 'Build It Yourself' game page, how-to-play notes

title: Webb's shade
text: The James Webb Space Telescope's major subsystems include its mirrors, science instruments, spacecraft bus and a large sunshield.
sourceLocations: NASA Science 'Scope It Out' game page, Webb observatory topics

title: Born in a university lab
text: CubeSats began in 1999 as a collaboration between Cal Poly San Luis Obispo and Stanford University to give university researchers affordable access to space.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 1 Introduction, p. 1

title: One unit = 10 cm
text: A 1U CubeSat is a 10 cm cube with a mass of roughly 1 to 1.33 kg; bigger CubeSats are built from multiple units, such as 3U and 6U.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 1 Introduction, p. 4

title: Months to years
text: A CubeSat can be built and delivered in as little as 9 months, but development typically takes 18 to 24 months.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 2 Development Process Overview, p. 9

title: Hitching a ride
text: NASA's CubeSat Launch Initiative gives selected CubeSats rides to space as auxiliary payloads on launches with spare capacity or by deployment from the International Space Station.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 1 Introduction, p. 2

title: Unfolding for sunlight
text: Many CubeSats use deployable solar panels to increase their exposure to the Sun; on one example spacecraft, deployable panels were expected to nearly double the power input.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 2, p. 16; ChargerSat-1 image caption

title: Point to power up
text: An attitude determination and control system (ADCS) stabilizes a spacecraft and points it in a chosen direction, for example aiming solar panels at the Sun or a camera at Earth.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 2, p. 17; Appendix glossary

title: Safe batteries
text: CubeSat developers generally prefer certified batteries, and launch providers review a battery report that checks the circuits protecting the batteries.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 2, p. 16; Chapter 6 Flight Certification Documentation, battery report section, p. 57

title: Power stays off until release
text: Separation switches keep a CubeSat's power system disconnected from its circuits while it sits inside the dispenser, so it cannot switch on too early.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 6 Flight Certification Documentation, p. 58

title: Someone has to listen
text: A CubeSat ground station needs at least a radio and an antenna, and CubeSat 101 warns that launching with an inadequate ground station is a mission killer.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 2, Ground Station Design, Development, and Testing, p. 22

title: A license to transmit
text: Most CubeSats need a radio license before they can transmit to the ground; in the United States the NTIA licenses government satellites and the FCC licenses non-federal ones.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 2 Licensing, p. 20; Chapter 5 Licensing Procedures

title: Shake before you fly
text: Verification testing typically includes vibration tests, which show a CubeSat will survive the shaking of launch, and thermal vacuum tests.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 2, p. 24; Chapter 6, Dynamic Environment Testing, p. 60

title: Bake it on the ground
text: A thermal vacuum bakeout heats a CubeSat in a vacuum so materials release contaminant gases on the ground rather than in space, where they could coat sensitive instruments.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 6, Thermal Vacuum Bakeout, p. 62

title: Leave space clean
text: Before launch, an orbital debris assessment shows that a CubeSat will not pose an unacceptable hazard to other spacecraft and will deorbit in a reasonable amount of time.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, Chapter 6, Orbital Debris Mitigation Compliance, p. 54

title: Sailing on sunlight
text: LightSail, a Planetary Society CubeSat launched through NASA's CubeSat Launch Initiative in 2015, tested deploying a 32-square-meter solar sail from a spacecraft about the size of a loaf of bread.
sourceLocations: CubeSat 101, LightSail image caption (ELaNa XI mission)
